analysis.body:
The five grid operators in this snapshot — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage sitting in interconnection queues as of August 31, 2026, spread across 8,381 individual requests. These are proposed projects that have asked to connect to the grid and are somewhere between early study and commissioning; they are not data center demand figures, and because each operator defines its queue scope differently, the totals are not directly addable into a single national number. ERCOT's queue alone accounts for 440,018 MW across 1,797 requests, with solar at roughly 151,883 MW, storage at about 160,906 MW, and gas at 76,751 MW; NYISO carries 319,095 MW but reports most of it — 291,136 MW — in an undifferentiated "other" category, making fuel-type comparison difficult there.

For readers tracking AI data center infrastructure, the fuel mix breakdown is the most telling signal. Battery storage and natural gas are the two resource types most closely associated with the around-the-clock, high-density load that large data center campuses create, because solar and wind alone cannot guarantee the continuous power such facilities require. Across the four operators that report storage separately, queued storage totals 160,906 MW at ERCOT, 68,429 MW at MISO, 53,412 MW at SPP, and 46,944 MW at CAISO; queued gas adds 76,751 MW, 30,236 MW, 47,392 MW, and 916 MW respectively at those same operators. That concentration of firm and storage capacity in Texas and the south-central region is consistent with where large hyperscale and AI campus announcements have clustered, though the queue data itself does not name end customers or confirm any project will be built.

The EIA commercial electricity sales figures for June 2026 offer a partial demand-side counterpoint, though they are a proxy for data center load rather than a direct measure of it, since data centers are billed mostly under the commercial class alongside other commercial users. Texas leads the eight states reported at 15,754 gigawatt-hours of commercial sales for the month, followed by California at 10,025 GWh and Virginia at 7,771 GWh; Virginia's figure is notable given its status as the largest data center market by facility count, and its average commercial price of 10.99 cents per kilowatt-hour sits well below California's 27.33 cents, which may help explain why queue activity in ERCOT territory dwarfs CAISO's 71,682 MW. The number to watch next is whether gas interconnection requests in ERCOT and SPP advance from study status to signed agreements, which would signal developers are confident enough in load commitments to absorb the cost of full interconnection studies.
